source.title: Decompose, Don't Expand: Capability-Independent AI Systems by Construction

record.tranche_reason: The paper measures task accuracy across differently sized models and reports flat or irregular model-size patterns for some tasks. This refines the downstream-predictability version, but it does not measure pretraining loss or test the original loss-scaling laws.
record.gate_note: The results concern 3D scene-editing task accuracy, not held-out pretraining cross-entropy, token or compute scaling, fitted power laws, or compute-optimal allocations. No rows are recorded for V1–V5 or V7. V6 is tested through task-accuracy comparisons across models. The paper also reports overall scores for the harness ladder in Table 2; those are omitted because the 60-row limit is used for per-task results from Tables 1 and 3.
record.test_reason: The within-family Qwen size sweep measures downstream task accuracy and therefore bears on V6 in a new setting. It provides descriptive size comparisons, without fitting or validating a predictive scaling relation. Flat scores on tasks transferred to a deterministic host do not establish absent scaling of language-model performance.
record.authors_conclusion: The record is broadly accurate, with qualifications: parity is guaranteed only for fully host-assigned components under the stated assumptions. Aggregate host-resolved scores include ambiguous model decisions and show Haiku and Opus deviations. Labelling remains model-dependent, with a non-monotonic local size trend and higher frontier scores. Only scene editing is measured; other domains are illustrative. Decomposition moves costs into building and maintaining the host and authored labels.
record.recipe_differences: The study evaluates downstream scene-editing task accuracy across model sizes and decomposes task components; it does not fit or test held-out-loss scaling laws, extrapolate from small pretraining runs, or optimize parameter-token allocation.
record.method_sensitivity: The observed outcomes differ by task and harness condition: host resolution flattens several task scores, while labelling remains variable. The paper also notes Haiku and Opus deviations under host resolution. Temperature=0 was not forwarded on the Anthropic client path, so frontier-model results were sampled rather than greedy.

fits_no_version.finding: After deterministic delegation, operation selection is 86% for all nine systems; selector resolution is 91% for eight; multi-op is 85% for seven. These are system outcomes after removing most relevant decisions from the model.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Delegating deterministic subtasks to a shared host can make their system-level accuracy largely independent of the model used for residual work.

fits_no_version.finding: Frontier models differ in argument extraction and labelling, but their parameter counts, training compute and pretraining losses are not reported.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Residual generative accuracy can differ between named models even when deterministic task components are shared.

record.problems: Evidence is from one domain and a small fixture set (9 to 22 fixtures per task). Most frontier cells are single runs, frontier models were sampled rather than run greedily, and the harness spans two system commits. Cross-domain examples are illustrative, not separately measured.
record.rows_left_out: To remain within 60 rows, omitted the remaining Table 1 scaffolded-baseline results: frontier-model entries and arg-extraction and multi-op entries. Also omitted Table 2 overall scores for the bare, scaffolded, constrained-output, and host-resolved harness ladder. These are reported in Section 3, Tables 1 and 2; the retained rows prioritize Table 3 per-task results and local baseline scores that display the reported non-monotonic model-size pattern.

untested.parts: Held-out pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens or compute; power-law form and range.
Prediction of larger-run loss from fits to small runs.
Architecture comparisons at fixed parameter count.
Power-law form in other modalities or training regimes; a scene-editing application alone does not test that form.
Quantitative predictive fits, held-out scale predictions, relations to pretraining loss, and controlled training-token or compute sweeps. Frontier model scales are undisclosed.
Dependence of fitted exponents or optimal allocations on setup and fitting choices; no scaling laws are fitted.

record.verdict_notes: All retained numerical values match the supplied tables. Row states describe size comparisons, not absolute accuracy or distance from 100%; the smallest local checkpoint is the reference. Repeated labelling values across harnesses are not independent scaling evidence. The original challenge label incorrectly includes the monotonically improving baseline operation-selection series. No result here challenges pretraining loss laws. Small fixture sets, limited repeats, sampled frontier outputs and two harness commits constrain interpretation. Results explicitly declared in rows_left_out are not listed as missing.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss as a function of parameters, tokens, or compute.
Whether power-law fits on small runs predict much larger runs.
Effects of depth, width, or other architecture choices at fixed parameter count.
Other modalities and training regimes, including repeated data, fine-tuning, and transfer.
The study measures task accuracy across model sizes in one 3D-editing domain; it does not compare performance with pretraining loss or evaluate a broader set of downstream benchmarks.
Dependence of scaling-law exponents or compute-optimal splits on fitting choices and training setup.
